'''Charles Felton Pidgin''' (November 11, 1844 – June 3, 1923) was an American author, statistician, and inventor.<ref name="ref1">Ayers, Herry Morgan. [http://www.bartleby.com/library/bios/4936.html The Reader’s Dictionary of Authors] (1917; 2015)</ref>  He is best known for his 1900 novel ''Quincy Adams Sawyer'', which became successful largely due to a big marketing campaign, and was adapted for the stage and silent film.

==Biography==
He was born on November 11, 1844, in [[Roxbury, Massachusetts]], to Mary E. Felton and Benjamin Gordon Pidgin.

As a young child, Pidgin was rendered lame by an accident to his hip, and he was also partially blind for a number of years.  He graduated from [[The English High School]] in Boston in 1863, and worked for ten years in the mercantile business.  He was appointed chief clerk of the Massachusetts Bureau of Labor Statistics in 1873.  In 1888 he independently published a book titled ''Practical Statistics''.   He was appointed as chief of the bureau in 1903, and remained there until 1907, leaving to focus on his writing work.<ref name="jstor"/><ref name="pop">Boyden, Frank L. [https://books.google.com/books?id=gyQQAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA27 Popular American Composers], ''Popular American Composers'', pp. 27-28 (1902)</ref>

In addition to serving as a state statistician, Pidgin remained busy in many other pursuits.  He invented statistical tabulating machines,<ref name="prince">[https://web.archive.org/web/20191222063243/http://findingaids.princeton.edu/names/131448100f7a444ce267c29687a6a419 Pidgin, Charles Felton, 1844-1923. - Finding Aid], princeton.edu, Retrieved 5 January 2016</ref> and wrote songs and musical comedies.  And he also became a fairly prolific author, for which he became best known.<ref name="numbers">(3 February 1917). [https://books.google.com/books?id=I0c0AQAAMAAJ&dq=%22&pg=RA11-PA47 Has the United States More than 118 Notable Composers?], ''Musical America'' (letter to editor where Pidgin combines his statistical skills with his musical interests to report how many composers appear in ''Who's Who in America'' and their ages)</ref>

On the stage, Pidgin's musical comedy adaptation of ''[[Peck's Bad Boy]]'' was first produced in 1883 and ran for many years.<ref name="pop"/>

His first and most popular novel ''Quincy Adams Sawyer'' was published in 1900 and sold over 250,000 copies.<ref name="books1">(16 September 1905). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1905/09/16/101706809.pdf Charles Felton Pidgin's Books], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref><ref name="sellingfast">(20 April 1901). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1901/04/20/106102641.pdf Notes and News (last item)], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (reporting that book is selling 2,000 copies per day)</ref><ref name="100Kcoming">(16 February 1901). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1901/02/16/102439573.pdf News and Notes (third item)], ''[[The New York Times]]'' (reporting that book sales are approaching 100,000 mark)</ref>  It was aggressively marketed by his publisher, C.M. Clark Publishing, run by [[Carro Morrell Clark|Carro Clark]], the wife of Pidgin's friend Charles Atkinson.<ref name="carr1">(2 March 1902). [http://cdnc.ucr.edu/cgi-bin/cdnc?a=d&d=LAH19020302.2.284.55 Woman Publisher Who Has Succeeded], ''Los Angeles Herald''</ref>  It was adapted into a popular stage play in 1902, which toured widely and played at the [[Academy of Music (New York City)|Academy of Music]] in New York.<ref name="qsadebut">(25 March 1902). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1902/03/25/101943696.pdf "Quincy Adams Sawyer" - Pidgin's Novel of New England Life Produced on Stage], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref><ref name="qsanyone">(8 August 1902). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1902/08/08/102433408.pdf "Quincy Adams Sawyer" - An Amusing Rustic Drama, with a City Chap for a Hero], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref><ref name="qsa2">(6 September 1902). [http://cambridge.dlconsulting.com/cgi-bin/cambridge?a=d&d=Tribune19020906-01.2.18# "Quincy Adams Sawyer" in a Week], ''Cambridge Tribune''</ref><ref name="qsaplay">(18 January 1904). [https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=266&dat=19040118&id=YENAAAAAIBAJ&sjid=jbIFAAAAIBAJ&pg=3161,6616930&hl=en At Opera House], ''[[Kentucky New Era]]''</ref><ref name="qsa3">(5 March 19070. [https://cdsun.library.cornell.edu/cgi-bin/cornell?a=d&d=CDS19070305.2.29.2&e=--------20--1-----all----# "Quincy Adams Sawyer"], ''The Cornell Daily Sun''</ref><ref name="qsa4">(9 May 1905). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1905/05/09/101413358.pdf "Quincy Adams Sawyer" - Rural Play, Elaborated, Seen at the Academy of Music], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>  The book was adapted to [[silent film]]s of the same name in 1912 (by Puritan Special Features Company, of which little is known),<ref name="mpw1">(10 January 1914). [https://books.google.com/books?id=UEs_AAAAYAAJ&pg=PA153 Pictures Stimulate Interest in Play], ''[[The Moving Picture World]]''</ref> and again in [[Quincy Adams Sawyer|1922]] starring [[John Bowers (actor)|John Bowers]], [[Blanche Sweet]], [[Lon Chaney]], and [[Barbara La Marr]].  Both films are considered lost.

Pidgin's next novel, ''Blennerhassett'' (1901), sold over 60,000 copies before even appearing in print.<ref name="blenner1">(June 1908). [https://books.google.com/books?id=GUREAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA182 Books], ''Sunset'', p. 182</ref>

Pidgin's 1902 novel ''The Climax: or, What Might Have Been: A Romance of the Great Republic'' envisioned an [[alternate history]] where [[Aaron Burr]] did not kill [[Alexander Hamilton]], and later became president.<ref name="weekly">Feeley, Gregory (6 September 2004). [https://web.archive.org/web/20160304220402/http://www.weeklystandard.com/the-way-it-wasnt/article/5740 The Way It Wasn't], ''The Weekly Standard''</ref><ref name="climax1"/>  Pidgin was an avid enthusiast of Burr, who he felt was wronged by history, and a number of his novels involve Burr.<ref name="littleburr"/>

[[File:Motion picture and method of producing the same 1917 US patent.png|right|thumb|Illustration from 1916 U.S. Patent application showing Pidgin's proposal to display silent film dialogue using balloons]] In 1916, Pidgin filed a patent application to display dialogue in silent films, proposing that actors inflate balloons or party favor-like objects with text on them to recreate the act of speaking.<ref name="companion">Cartmell, Deborah. [https://books.google.com/books?id=63y9jREP6QEC&pg=PT74 A Companion to Literature, Film and Adaptation] (2012)</ref>  The idea never took off, and this proposal has only received modern attention as being a rather ludicrous idea.<ref name="felton">Felton, Bruce. [http://help.lockergnome.com/movies/Odd-Movie-Patent--ftopict17469.html What Were They Thinking? Really Bad Ideas Throughout History] (2003)</ref><ref name="nontalking">Ptak, John F. (28 January 2014). [http://longstreet.typepad.com/thesciencebookstore/2014/01/the-non-talking-talkie-soundless-talking-pictures-1917.html The Non-Talking Talkie--Soundless Talking Pictures (1917) and the Beauty of Timelessly Bad Ideas], ''JF Ptak Science Books''</ref><ref name="absurd">(30 January 2014). [http://www.neatorama.com/2014/01/30/An-Absurd-Device-to-Add-Dialogue-to-Silent-Films/ An Absurd Device to Add Dialogue to Silent Films], ''Neatorama''</ref>

Pidgin married three times.  He married his first wife Lizzie Abbott Dane in 1867, and she died the following year.  In 1873 he married Lucy Sturtevant Gardner, who became a doctor and practiced medicine until her death in 1896.<ref name="deathlucy">(20 June 1896). [http://cambridge.dlconsulting.com/cgi-bin/cambridge?a=d&d=Chronicle18960620-01.2.39# Death of Dr. Lucy S. Pidgin], ''Cambridge Chronicle''</ref><ref name="deathlucybigger">(27 June 1896). [http://cambridge.dlconsulting.com/cgi-bin/cambridge?a=d&d=Chronicle18960627-01.2.63# A Friend of the Sick and Unfortunate - Death or Mrs. Dr. Lucy Pidgin Mourned by a Wife Circle of Friends - a Sketch of her Life and Work], ''Cambridge Chronicle''</ref>  His third wife, married in 1897, was Frances Fern Douglas.<ref name="biographacy">[https://books.google.com/books?id=THRMAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA479 The National Cyclopedia of American Biography, Vol. 13], pp. 479-80 (1906)</ref><ref name="thirdmarriage">(24 July 1897). [http://cambridge.dlconsulting.com/cgi-bin/cambridge?a=d&d=Tribune18970724-01.2.58&srpos=5&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-charles+pidgin-----# Pidgin-Douglas], ''Cambridge Chronicle''</ref>  Pidgin died at his home in [[Melrose Highlands, Massachusetts]], on June 3, 1923.<ref name="jstor">[https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Felton_Pidgin_%281844-1923%29_obituary_in_Journal_of_the_American_Statistical_Association_%281923%29.png Miscellaneous Notes - Charles Felton Pidgin],  ''Journal of the American Statistical Association'', Vol. 18, No. 143 (Sep., 1923), pp. 919-924</ref><ref name="phillyinquiry">(5 June 1923). [http://fultonhistory.com/Newspapers%2023/Philadelphia%20PA%20Inquirer/Philadelphia%20PA%20Inquirer%201923/Philadelphia%20PA%20Inquirer%201923%20-%203578.pdf Charles F. Pidgin (death notice)], ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]''</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Charles F. Pidgin Dead. Author of "Quincy Adams Sawyer". Also a Statistical Writer |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1923/06/05/archives/charles-f-pidgin-dead-author-of-quineyadayns-sawyer-also-a.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 5, 1923}}</ref>

==List of novels==
[[File:Charles F. Pidgin and Charles D. Blake (Boston Public Library).jpg|right|thumb|Cover of "Selections from the Operatic Works of Chas F. Pidgin and Chas D. Blake", 1889]]
* ''Quincy Adams Sawyer and Mason's Corner Folks'' (1900)
* ''Blennerhassett'' (1901)<ref name="atheron1">[[Gertrude Atherton|Atherton, Gertrude]]. (12 October 1901). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1901/10/12/102627877.pdf Mr. Pidgin and Alexander Hamilton (letter to editor)], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref><ref name="listof">Smith, Geoffrey D. [https://books.google.com/books?id=HPYP-a0hjLsC&pg=PA532 American Fiction, 1901-1925: A Bibliography], p. 532-33 (Cambridge Press 1997)</ref><ref name="blenner">(26 October 1901). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1901/10/26/101084545.pdf Hamilton and Burr - Mr. Pidgin Replies to Miss Atherton's Criticism of "Blennerhassett"], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>
* ''Stephen Holton'' (1902)<ref name="holton1">(3 May 1902). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1902/05/03/118469362.pdf Mr. Pidgin's "Stephen Holton"], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>
* ''The Climax'' (1902)<ref name="climax1">(2 October 1902). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1902/10/04/101288876.pdf The Climax (review)], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>
* ''The Letter H'' (1904)
* ''A Nation's Idol'' (1904)
* ''Little Burr, the Warwick of America'' (1905) (inspired by [[Jeremiah Clemens]]'s ''The Rivals'' (1859))<ref name="littleburr">(22 April 1905). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1905/04/22/101358882.pdf A Novel of Aaron Burr], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>
* ''The Corsican Lovers'' (1906)
* ''Sarah Bernhardt Brown'' (1906)
* ''The Hidden Man'' (1906)
* ''The Toymakers'' (1907)
* ''Labor'' (1908)
* ''Theodosia'' (1908) (about [[Theodosia Burr Alston]], daughter of Aaron Burr)<ref name="theo1">(25 January 1908). [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1908/01/25/104716269.pdf Wide Variety in Forthcoming Books], ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>
* ''The Further Adventures of Quincy Adams Sawyer and Mason Corner Folks'' (1909)
* ''The Chronicles of Quincy Adams Sawyer, detective'' (1912)
* ''The House of Shame'' (1912)
